anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Inefficient or over-broad application SQL and transaction design that forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic truly requires.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory, parallelism, checkpoint, etc.) that are out of line with hardware capacity, workload mix, or version defaults, independently of actual resource limits.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Aggregate in-engine memory areas grow beyond the safe operating envelope, causing OS pressure, paging, or OOM events.

When these three root causes coexist, the workload issues, the engine settings, and the host-level memory footprint all collide. Inefficient statements run in larger, longer transactions, each granted overly generous work or sort buffers by mis-configured parameters; as concurrency rises, aggregate memory skyrockets past physical limits. The system then shows a mixed symptom pattern: explosive resident-set growth, sudden paging or cgroup kills, erratic spikes of CPU spin on memory reconciliation, checkpoint and log-flush storms that do not align with I/O utilization, long-tail query latencies, application timeouts, and a flood of slow-query and out-of-memory entries in logs. Observability is clouded because waits oscillate between memory pressure, log I/O, and lock contention, making any single diagnostic view appear inconsistent or misleading.

Causally, the sub-optimal SQL drives high intermediate result volumes and longer transaction lifetimes. Mis-sized configuration parameters—such as excessive per-query work memory, inflated parallel-worker counts, or an oversized buffer pool—allocate disproportionately large chunks of RAM to each bloated operation. The cumulative effect breaches physical memory, triggering OS paging or OOM killers that evict useful pages and terminate processes. Memory pressure, in turn, forces aggressive background flushing and checkpoint activity, amplifying I/O waits and extending the runtime of the already inefficient statements. The feedback loop between chatty or data-heavy SQL, over-generous configuration settings, and runaway memory allocation magnifies performance instability and obscures the primary culprit, leading to systemic slowdown or even node failure across both transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_description: Unable to handle the donor's view change uuid transaction information when initializing the conflict detection component. Possible out of memory error.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with insufficient memory headroom, buffer pressure, oversized intermediate state, or memory-allocation constraints inside the engine or client library.
entry.solution_guidance: Check memory availability, per-session memory settings, large sorts or hashes, and whether workload concurrency is amplifying memory consumption.
